subject: zoology
question_text: Compare the adaptations of animals with freshwater and seawater mode of life.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.47, SAQ 57). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: The freshwater problem
lines: Fresh water holds less salt than the body
fluids of the animals living in it.
So water passes INTO their bodies through
the body surface. This is endosmosis.
A freshwater animal therefore has to remove
the extra water that keeps entering.
steps.why: Both halves of this answer are the same story told in opposite directions, so the problem is stated first in each half; every adaptation that follows is a way of solving that one problem.
common_mistakes: Writing that fresh water is saltier than the body. It holds LESS salt than the body fluids.
Using the word exosmosis here. Water moves IN, so it is endosmosis.
steps.memory_tip: Water always moves towards the saltier side. In fresh water the animal is the salty side, so water comes in.
steps.margin_note: State the direction of the water first. Every adaptation below answers it.

steps.label: Freshwater adaptations
lines: (i) Freshwater fishes have glomerular
kidneys, which remove the excess water as a
large amount of dilute urine.
(ii) Freshwater sponges produce gemmules to
survive the summer.
(iii) The African lung fish undergoes
aestivation by forming a gelatinous cocoon
to survive the summer.
steps.why: The first adaptation answers the water problem directly; the other two answer a second freshwater problem — a pond may dry up — which is why they are about surviving the summer and not about salt.
common_mistakes: Writing that freshwater fishes have aglomerular kidneys. Those belong to the MARINE fishes.
Leaving out the gemmules and the cocoon. Drying up is a freshwater problem too.
steps.memory_tip: Glomerular kidney for the water, gemmule and cocoon for the dry season.
steps.margin_note: Three adaptations, one line each. Keep the kidney first.

steps.label: The seawater problem
lines: Sea water holds more salt than the body
fluids of the animals living in it.
So water passes OUT of their bodies. This is
exosmosis.
A marine animal therefore keeps losing water
and has to save it.
steps.why: Writing this half in the same shape as the freshwater half makes the comparison the question asks for visible on the page, with only the direction of the water changed.
common_mistakes: Using endosmosis here. In sea water the water moves OUT, so it is exosmosis.
Writing that marine animals gain water. They lose it continuously.
steps.memory_tip: Same rule, opposite direction: the sea is the salty side, so the water leaves the animal.
steps.margin_note: Mirror the freshwater half exactly, with the direction reversed.

steps.label: Seawater adaptations

lines.text: Fresh water: take it in. Sea water: keep it

lines: (i) Marine fishes have aglomerular kidneys
with fewer nephrons, so little water is
lost as urine.
(ii) They have salt-secreting chloride cells
in the gills, which throw out the extra
salt.
(iii) Marine birds and penguins pass out
salt drops through the nostrils.
(iv) Sharks retain urea and trimethylamine
oxide (TMO) in the body fluids to keep the
salt balance.
steps.why: Four adaptations are given because they solve two different sides of the same problem — saving water and getting rid of salt — and an answer with only the kidney has covered one side.
common_mistakes: Writing that marine fishes pass a lot of urine. They pass very little, to save water.
Leaving out the shark. Retaining urea and TMO is the named example in this answer.
steps.memory_tip: Two jobs at sea: hold the water in (kidney) and push the salt out (gills, nostrils).
steps.margin_note: Four adaptations, one line each. The box states the whole comparison in one line.

insider_note: The question says compare, so write the two halves in the same order with the same headings — a page of freshwater adaptations followed by nothing on the sea scores half.
